claims.text: Al0.3CoCrFeNi can exist as a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy.
The proposed initial HEA is chemically homogeneous.
The proposed HEA has a grain structure that permits both dislocation slip and deformation-twin formation.
Ballistic or other high-rate deformation of HEAs can produce both dislocations and deformation twins.
Twin density increases with strain rate at an equivalent imposed strain.
At high strain rates, elevated local stress and thermal effects promote rapid deformation-twin nucleation.
Large plastic deformation converts plastic work into heat and can raise the material temperature.
Thermal softening can overcome strain hardening and strain-rate hardening, causing localized plastic flow.
Deformation twins act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion.
Twin–dislocation interactions increase strain hardening and delay shear localization.
The cooperative action of twinning and dislocation slip enhances strength and ductility during dynamic loading.
Compared with quasi-static deformation or a twin-suppressed variant, the high-rate HEA will have a higher strain-hardening rate.
Compared with the baseline, the high-rate HEA will show a measurable increase in deformation-twin density.
Compared with the baseline, the high-rate HEA will exhibit a delayed onset of shear localization or failure.
The proposed mechanism becomes dominant above approximately 10^-2 s^-1.
The mechanism applies primarily to HEAs whose stacking-fault energy and microstructure support deformation twinning.
Significantly elevated temperature or compositional and microstructural suppression of twinning can eliminate the proposed effect.
Grain-size refinement or minor alloying adjustments can be used to suppress deformation twinning in the comparison alloy.
The fracture strain of the Cantor alloy is strain-rate-sensitive over 10^-3 to 10 s^-1 at high temperatures, whereas its yield strength is comparatively rate-insensitive.
